title: Restating a problem with a list input
idea: MEET: when the input is a LIST, the restatement should say what one item is, how many there are (len), and what per-item rule applies.

exercises.prompt: PROBLEM: 'Given a list of prices, count how many are above 20.' What is ONE item in the input?
exercises.explanation: The input is a list; one item is a single price. Knowing what one item is tells you what the per-item rule tests.

exercises.prompt: In that problem, the per-item RULE is...
exercises.explanation: For each price you ask 'is it above 20?'. The per-item rule is the test you apply to every item.

exercises.prompt: With a list input, it helps to name what a single item is before planning.
exercises.explanation: Yes — once you know one item is 'a price', the loop body writes itself: do the rule to each price.

exercises.prompt: Which tool tells you HOW MANY items a list has?
exercises.explanation: len() gives the size of a list — introduced back in Unit 53. It answers 'how many items?'.

exercises.prompt: Select the true statements about a list input for 'average the scores'.
options: One item is a single score
The number of items is len(scores)
The per-item step adds the score to a running total
One item is the whole list
exercises.explanation: One item is a score; len gives the count; each item feeds the running total. The last option confuses item with list.

exercises.prompt: Why does naming 'one item' matter for a list problem?
options: The loop body is a rule applied to one item at a time
exercises.explanation: A for-loop visits one item at a time, so your plan is really 'what do I do to ONE item?' repeated.

exercises.prompt: A list of 5 prices and a list of 50 prices need completely different plans.
exercises.explanation: No — the plan is the same per-item rule in a loop. Only the length differs. That's the power of looping.

exercises.prompt: Match each list problem to its per-item rule.

pairs.right: add this score to the total
is this item bigger than the best so far?

exercises.explanation: Each list problem is a per-item rule repeated in a loop. Naming the rule is half the plan.

exercises.prompt: Order the restatement habit for a list input.
blocks: State the per-item rule you'll apply
exercises.explanation: One item, how many, the per-item rule. With those three named, the loop almost writes itself.

options: For a list input, name one item, its count, and the per-item rule
Lists must be planned item by item with different plans each time
A list input has no items
exercises.explanation: List problems reduce to a per-item rule in a loop. Restating that way makes big lists feel small.
